The Orange weaver Ploceus aurantius is a passerine species common in the coastal and mangrove regions of West Africa, and recent respirometry studies have provided valuable data on its metabolic physiology. Under controlled laboratory conditions, the basal metabolic rate of adult individuals was calculated from oxygen consumption measurements taken during the inactive phase of the daily cycle. These measurements, conducted at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], revealed a resting oxygen uptake of approximately 39.4 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 39.4 milliliters per hour], a value that aligns well with the allometric predictions for ploceid finches of comparable size. This relatively modest metabolic demand is consistent with a foraging lifestyle centered on seeds and small invertebrates, which generally requires lower daily energetic expenditure than a purely insectivorous diet. The experimental setup ensured that all birds were post-absorptive and at rest, thus meeting the standard criteria for basal metabolic rate determination. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of the energetic costs associated with thermoregulation in a humid tropical environment.

The early developmental stages of the Orange weaver are characterized by a relatively rapid progression from hatching to nutritional independence. Newly hatched nestlings emerge from incubated eggs at a very small size, with an initial wet weight upon hatching of 2.22 grams [Ww0 = 2.22 grams], a mass that primarily reflects the residual yolk reserves and the hydration state of the altricial chick. This initial mass is typical of many weaver species, whose altricial young require intensive brooding and frequent provisioning. The incubation period itself, during which the developing embryo relies entirely on the egg's endogenous nutrients, lasts for approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days] when eggs are maintained at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This duration is consistent with the 13 to 14 day range reported in the literature for congeneric species, and the specific incubation temperature reflects the mean nest microclimate recorded in field conditions. The brevity of this embryonic phase underscores the trade-off between rapid hatching and the altricial state of the neonate.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the period from hatching to the achievement of sustained flight, or fledging, spans approximately 14.5 days since birth [tx = approximately 14.5 days since birth]. During this interval, the chick undergoes substantial feather development and muscular strengthening. Following fledging, the young bird continues to undergo somatic growth and physiological maturation, and the onset of puberty, defined by the capacity for gamete production, occurs at about 43.5 days after hatching [tp = about 43.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity is characteristic of many tropical passerines, allowing them to exploit favorable breeding conditions that may be ephemeral. The precise timing of these life-history events is critical for synchronizing reproduction with peak food availability.

Reproductive investment in the Orange weaver is characterized by a moderate output per breeding attempt, as females typically produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and usually complete one successful clutch each year [F_R_i = one successful clutch each year]. This reproductive rate is interpreted as a trade-off between offspring quality and the energetic demands of incubation and chick-rearing. The age at which females first participate in such reproductive activity is a significant demographic parameter; field studies indicate that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 547.5 days since birth [tR = approximately 547.5 days since birth], recorded under natural environmental conditions averaging 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay of over a year before the initiation of breeding allows young birds to acquire sufficient body reserves and a suitable nesting territory. The combination of a moderate clutch size and a single annual breeding event suggests a relatively slow life-history strategy compared to some multi-brooded congeneric species, potentially constrained by the unpredictable availability of nest-building materials and insect prey.

Adult body size in Ploceus aurantius exhibits a subtle but consistent sexual dimorphism, most evident in the maximum recorded body masses. Females attain a larger ultimate wet weight, with adults reaching approximately 25 grams [Wwi = approximately 25 grams], whereas males typically achieve a slightly lower maximum adult body mass of about 23.7 grams [Wwi = about 23.7 grams]. This reverse sexual size dimorphism, where the female is the larger sex, is somewhat unusual among weavers but may relate to the energetic costs associated with egg production and extended incubation bouts. Despite their smaller body size, males invest considerable energy in nest construction and territorial defense. With a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 8.9 years [am = approximately 8.9 years] under a thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the Orange weaver demonstrates a longevity that aligns with slow-paced life-history strategies typical of tropical island passerines. This combination of distinct adult masses and a relatively long lifespan situates the species within a slow-paced life-history continuum.
